strengths: Clear methodological contribution: Per-timestep score-space supervision is well-motivated and clearly shown to improve upon final-sample-only supervision, as demonstrated in toy experiments (Figure 1)
Rigorous theoretical framework: Correct derivation from Bradley-Terry preferences to score-space objective; demonstrates Diffusion DPO as special case; appropriate approximations
Practical solution eliminating human annotation bottleneck: Prompt perturbation strategy is clever; efficient variant requires no explicit negative image generation

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple dimensions: Multiple architectures (SD-1.4, SDXL, SANA), tasks (alignment and aesthetic), metrics (GenEval, CompBench, HPSv2, PickScore), and thorough ablations on dataset size, hyperparameters, and perturbation strategies
Strong data efficiency: Achieves competitive results with 10K-200K pairs; comparable performance to methods using human annotations (Itercomp, CaPO) without relying on such data
Broad architectural support: Demonstrated effectiveness on U-Net and DiT/flow-matching models
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, effective visualizations, and comprehensive supplementary material with full derivations and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited applicability of prompt perturbation strategy: Core assumption (degraded prompts lead to lower-quality images) not systematically validated; simplistic token removal approach; generalization to non-text-to-image domains unclear (e.g., audio, video)

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Requires task-specific tuning of β (e.g., 16000 for SDXL vs. 2000 for SANA); no principled guidance provided; acknowledged but not adequately addressed for practical deployment

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Preference datasets from Itercomp/CaPO unavailable, making fair comparison difficult; DSPO+CPP missing from aesthetic experiments; no human evaluation—reliance on automatic metrics may miss important quality aspects

Gap between theory and practice: Practical instantiation using prompt perturbations differs substantially from theoretical contrastive policy pair formulation; decomposition in Eq. 27 lacks deep justification; sensitivity to reference model quality unexplored

Incremental contribution relative to Diffusion DPO: Core advance is adding per-timestep supervision; while solid, the novelty is somewhat limited; improvements over baselines, though consistent, are modest in some cases (e.g., GenEval 0.5229→0.6049 vs. Itercomp 0.6108)

Limited failure mode and robustness analysis: No systematic investigation of when prompt degradation fails; insufficient analysis of what makes stepwise supervision effective across different timesteps; no discussion of robustness to poor-quality degraded prompts

Incomplete ablations: No analysis of downstream task dependence on reference model quality; unclear how performance varies with different perturbation quality; joint improvement setup (Appendix C) underdeveloped
Computational overhead underemphasized: 25% additional computation per step; data generation costs (5 H100-days) not amortized; training time comparisons with baselines missing

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: extends DPO from final-sample to stepwise supervision in score space with dense learning signals throughout the denoising trajectory
Practical approach eliminates need for expensive human-labeled preference data or trained reward models by using prompt perturbation for pseudo-preference generation
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (SD-1.4, SDXL, SANA) and tasks (alignment, aesthetic quality) with data efficiency advantages (200K vs 800K+ pairs)
Solid mathematical foundation with clear derivation from Bradley-Terry model through DPO to score-space formulation and well-articulated connections to related work
Consistent improvements across all tested architectures and benchmarks with effective qualitative results demonstrating visual improvements
Thorough supplementary material with implementation details, ablation studies, and extensive qualitative comparisons enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Insufficient theoretical justification for prompt perturbation as a proxy for human preferences: the assumption that degraded prompts yield less desirable outputs is reasonable but lacks rigorous empirical validation against actual human preferences

Limited theoretical understanding of why stepwise supervision works; the counterintuitive finding (Table 6) that unpaired prompts and images work nearly as well as paired ones undermines the central narrative about supervision quality and signal density

Missing human evaluation: evaluation relies entirely on automated metrics (GenEval, T2I-CompBench) which depend on other models with known biases; no validation that improvements translate to human-perceived quality

Modest empirical improvements in some cases: Table 1 shows GenEval improvement of only 0.007 over DSPO+CPP with marginal changes in CompBench, and improvements lack statistical significance testing or error bars

Hyperparameter sensitivity: requires task and model-specific tuning (β = 16000 for SD/SDXL vs 2000 for SANA; random removal vs LLaMA for different tasks), limiting practical applicability and adding design complexity

Incomplete analysis of computational costs: while claiming data efficiency, the method requires 25% more computation per training step; full cost comparison versus alternatives (800K pairs with Diffusion DPO vs 200K with DDSPO over 100 steps) not fully amortized

Limited failure case analysis: paper acknowledges prompt perturbation is not applicable in some settings but provides no concrete examples, characterization of failure modes, or guidance on when the approach is appropriate
Scope limitations: evaluated only on text-to-image generation; applicability to other modalities (audio, 3D) and settings with very different reference model architectures remains unclear

Missing ablations on reference model quality, forward process approximation impact (Eq. 27), and systematic comparison of perturbation strategies across tasks rather than using different strategies per task

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation that identifies genuine limitations in forward-process approximations used by existing methods like Diffusion DPO
Rigorous mathematical foundation with clear derivations connecting Bradley-Terry preference modeling to stepwise contrastive supervision of diffusion transitions
Dual practical instantiations (DD-CPP and TF-CPP) demonstrating flexibility - particularly TF-CPP's ability to improve models without preference-labeled data is valuable
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple tasks, benchmarks, and architectures with consistent improvements shown across SD-1.4, SDXL, SANA, and SD3-Medium
Thorough ablation studies examining dataset size effects, prompt degradation strategies, and hyperparameter sensitivity with detailed supplementary results
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation notes, training configurations, and commitment to code release
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: applying Bradley-Terry formulation to intermediate denoising steps is a straightforward extension of DPO principles with limited conceptual advance over Diffusion DPO
Critical hyperparameter sensitivity requiring careful β tuning across different tasks/architectures (β ∈ {8000, 16000}) with no principled selection guidance, acknowledged as practical limitation
TF-CPP engineering complexity: quality heavily depends on prompt degradation strategy choice without principled method to select best strategy, undermining 'training-free' claim
Modest empirical gains with many improvements being incremental (e.g., Table 1: 0.5045 vs 0.5045) despite added complexity; statistical significance often unclear
Limited evaluation scope: over-reliance on automatic metrics with limited human evaluation (450 judgments), missing assessments of diversity, inference speed, and robustness
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SPO and SoftREPA comparisons relegated to appendix, with SoftREPA showing competitive/better performance in some metrics
Insufficient analysis of why stepwise supervision helps with limited intuition about practical benefits; Section 3.4's claim about removing forward-process reliance not convincingly demonstrated
Critical dependency on preference data quality underexplored; DD-CPP requires 200K synthetic preferences whose construction quality impacts results
Data-Driven aspect requires careful construction of preference pairs; TF-CPP cost of generating and evaluating pseudo-preference pairs not clearly quantified
Missing practical guidance: limited discussion of computational overhead, minimal guidance on choosing between DD-CPP and TF-CPP variants, no analysis of failure modes

strengths: Novel framework for stepwise preference supervision over intermediate denoising transitions, addressing a genuine limitation in existing DPO-style methods for diffusion models
Rigorous mathematical formulation with well-justified approximations using Jensen's inequality and careful derivation of the DDSPO objective
Two practical instantiations (DD-CPP and TF-CPP) offering valuable trade-offs between data requirements and computational efficiency
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (SD-1.4, SDXL, SANA, SD3-Medium), benchmarks (GenEval, T2i-CompBench), and metrics (alignment and aesthetic quality)
Consistent improvements demonstrated across diverse settings with data efficiency studies, ablation studies on degradation strategies, and human evaluation confirming preferences
Training-free variant (TF-CPP) enables preference optimization without preference-labeled data, significantly broadening applicability
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details, transparent discussion of limitations, and robustness analysis across multiple generation seeds
Practical impact shown through gains on both text-to-image alignment and aesthetic quality metrics across multiple model architectures
weaknesses: Significant hyperparameter sensitivity requiring careful per-task tuning of β coefficient that controls quality-alignment trade-off, reducing plug-and-play applicability
Measurable computational overhead (5.2% increase for DD-CPP, additional evaluation costs for TF-CPP) that adds practical deployment burden
Limited core technical novelty—primarily extends existing DPO framework to intermediate steps; Bradley-Terry formulation and diffusion-model application largely follow prior work

Contrastive policy pair quality heavily depends on perturbation strategy (Table 4 shows significant variation across LLaMA, Random-removal, etc.), suggesting benefits partially tied to engineering choices rather than core method
Method still requires substantial computational resources (200K pseudo-preference pairs for TF-CPP, pretrained reference model) despite training-free framing
Modest absolute improvements in many metrics (often 0.3-0.5 points on GenEval/CompBench) raising questions about practical significance despite statistical consistency
Limited exploration of failure modes and settings where stepwise supervision may not help; no discussion of prompt types or objectives where method underperforms
Incomplete baseline comparisons—SoftREPA uses public checkpoint not fair reproduction, SPO not deeply analyzed, some recent preference optimization methods potentially missing
